claims.text: An ML-enhanced AIMD framework with thermodynamic integration can accurately determine melting and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the high-entropy-alloy family.
The proposed framework can determine these properties more efficiently than traditional approaches.
The target HEA solid exhibits significant atomic disorder.
The ML potential is trained on DFT data and combined with thermodynamic integration for sampling near melting.
The simulations will use an NPT ensemble at temperatures approaching the melting point.
Adequately sized periodic supercells can represent HEA compositional disorder.
The ML potential captures the local atomic environments typical of HEAs.
The ML potential captures bond-order variations typical of HEAs.
Capturing these local environments and bond-order variations provides DFT-level accuracy.
Use of the ML potential reduces computational cost.
The ML-enhanced simulation can sample high-temperature configurations efficiently while retaining fidelity to quantum-mechanical interactions.
Thermodynamic integration converts the sampled configurations into accurate melting and fusion thermodynamics.
Predicted melting temperatures, fusion enthalpies, fusion entropies, melting volume changes, and liquid-phase properties will be within approximately 5% of experimental values.
The approximately 5% accuracy will hold over a diverse compositional range of HEAs.
Traditional DFT-only approaches are computationally prohibitive for extensive compositional sampling of HEAs.
Failure of the training data to include rare or complex local atomic environments can reduce model accuracy.
Instability of thermodynamic integration near second-order transitions can reduce prediction accuracy.
Incomplete training coverage or unstable thermodynamic integration may produce errors exceeding 10%.
Under ideal conditions, the estimated prediction error is approximately plus or minus 5%.
Consistent deviations greater than 5% across multiple HEA compositions would falsify the claimed predictive accuracy.
